findings.what: Screen 6's sweep ends with the Battery current readout at 2.5 A for D = 25%, and screen 10 ends with 20.0 A for Boost at 50%, which are exactly the answers to the next screens' puzzles, so hide the battery current on those two demonstrations (or until each puzzle is solved).

findings.where: Screen 4 (Two areas), and the same step in explain.text paragraph 3
findings.what: The step from 'the current ends each cycle where it began' to 'the two areas must be equal' skips the one link that makes it true: each shaded area divided by L is how far the current climbs or falls (v = L di/dt turned round), so add that sentence before 'So the two areas must be equal'.

The words say 'Flip the picker to Boost', but the screen opens with Boost already chosen and the output already rising from 48 V, so the instruction contradicts what Dan sees; say 'The picker now shows Boost' or open the screen in Buck.

It carries nine footnotes, most on plain description ([^2] what a buck is, [^3] the freewheel path, [^7] and [^8] the boost's on and off states, [^1], [^9]), against the at-most-a-few rule; keep the zero-average rule ([^4]) and the 20% to 40% value ([^6]) and drop the rest.

Each is at 89 words, and the caption under the picture adds about 25 to 30 more, so both screens are at the ceiling; screen 8 especially packs two formulas, a worked number, the guide, the capacitor's job and an instruction, and could lose the rate sentence or the capacitor sentence.

A higher frequency is offered as a free cure for ripple ('Raise the frequency, and the ripple shrinks', 'A higher frequency or a bigger inductor brings it back'), but lesson 4 taught that switching heat climbs with frequency, so one sentence should name that cost to keep the trade honest.

'A good first estimate is 20% to 40% of the output current' does not say what is being estimated and reads as a prediction, so say the ripple is usually chosen to be 20% to 40% of the output current; screen 9 then calls it a guide.
'the current ramps half as far each way, 1.2 A in all' reads as up plus down totalling 1.2 A, when it climbs 1.2 A and falls 1.2 A, so say that.

It jumps from Vin × D = (Vout − Vin) × (1 − D) straight to Vout = Vin ÷ (1 − D) without the multiply-out line the buck got on screen 6, so add 'The Vin × D terms cancel, leaving Vin = Vout × (1 − D).'
'The area above is (Vin − Vout) × D' drops the cycle time that screen 4's 'a voltage times a time' implies, so add that each is also times T, which cancels.
'Both come to 36' has no unit, so give the areas as 48 V × 15 µs and 144 V × 5 µs, both 720 V·µs, at the picture's 50 kHz.

findings.where: Screen 1 (Heat in a transistor), the picture
findings.what: The question is about a transistor held part on, but the picture already shows the finished buck converter with its switch, diode and labelled on/off plots, which nothing has introduced yet; hide the plots, or show only the battery, transistor and load until the right Check.
The Ripple readout and its 'Ripple guide for a buck' band show from screen 2, six screens before ripple is taught on screen 8, so hide them until then to keep the early screens calm.
The brief's last screen, an inverter leg as a buck whose D follows a sine, the bridge into lesson 7, appears only in explain.text, so add it as one sentence to the finish words.

Nothing ties the 48 V battery example to Dan's world; one sentence that DC/DC converters feed lower-voltage DC loads from a ship's DC supply or battery (the brief's ABS note) would show why this matters at sea.
At laptop width the lesson column sits against the left of the card with the right half empty, so centre .pz with margin-inline: auto.
